headlines.article_text: Bank Indonesia faces pressure to hike as MSCI alarm pressures rupiah Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Bank Indonesia is under pressure to raise its benchmark rate on Wednesday to stabilize the rupiah. Economists are split on the size of a hike, with Citi expecting a 50-basis-point hike to 6.25% and Capital Economics and others seeing a smaller increase to 6%. Analysts urge credible market governance reforms to address MSCI's fundamental concerns. In this article MSCI Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Destry Damayanti, governor of Bank Indonesia, during a news conference with Suahasil Nazara, Indonesia's finance minister, at the central bank's headquarters in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah. Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June. MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia to "standalone" from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index. Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year. "Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure." Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks. The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to a three-month high of 3.28% in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of $146.3 billion at the end of September would be adequate to stabilize the rupiah. Market integrity in question "Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added. The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital. Josua Pardede Chief economist, PT Bank Permata An MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June. "BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images India's Jio Platforms has seen the anchor investor quota for its initial public offering oversubscribed more than 30 times, according to a source familiar with the matter, drawing bids from top asset managers including BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC. The country's largest telecommunications and digital services company, backed by Meta and Google, plans to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through India's largest ever IPO in rupee terms . Jio Platforms, in a release on Monday, said it had finalized the allocation of 72.47 million equity shares to anchor investors at 1,119 rupees a share, at the upper range of the price band. The anchor book is a portion of the total fundraise set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding. Some other major institutional investors who have been allocated shares include India's state-owned insurance firm Life Insurance Corporation , Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan Asset Management and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. The Jio Platforms IPO will be open to the public from Wednesday through Friday. Jio Platforms, owned by Reliance Industries , has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider .
